questions.q: What is the main practical difference between a platform-managed key and a customer-managed key (CMK)?
options: A CMK uses a stronger encryption algorithm than a platform-managed key
A CMK gives the customer independent control to revoke or rotate the key, separate from the cloud provider
Platform-managed keys only exist on AWS, never on Azure
A CMK means the data is no longer encrypted at rest at all
questions.explain: Both models encrypt data the same way; the difference is control. With a CMK in Key Vault or KMS, the customer can independently revoke access to the key — immediately making the data unreadable — which a platform-managed key does not allow.

questions.q: Which S3 server-side encryption mode means AWS never stores the encryption key at all?
options: SSE-S3
SSE-KMS with an AWS-managed key
SSE-C
Default encryption with no key specified
questions.explain: SSE-C requires the customer to supply the encryption key on every request; AWS uses it to encrypt/decrypt but never stores it, which also means losing the key makes the data permanently unreadable.

questions.q: By default, does an Azure storage account or an S3 bucket reject plain HTTP connections?
options: No — encryption in transit must be explicitly enforced, via "Require secure transfer" on Azure Storage or a bucket policy denying non-TLS requests on S3
Yes, both reject HTTP automatically with no configuration needed
Only Azure enforces this by default; S3 has no way to enforce TLS at all
Only S3 enforces this by default; Azure Storage has no equivalent setting
questions.explain: Encryption at rest being on by default does not mean encryption in transit is enforced. Azure Storage needs "Require secure transfer" turned on, and S3 needs a bucket policy denying requests where aws:SecureTransport is false.

questions.q: Which Azure feature is customer-managed by design rather than an optional upgrade from a platform-managed default?
options: Azure Disk Encryption, which stores its BitLocker/dm-crypt keys in Key Vault
Storage Service Encryption for blob storage
Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) for Azure SQL Database
Azure's default TLS certificate for App Service
questions.explain: Azure Disk Encryption layers BitLocker (Windows) or dm-crypt (Linux) on VM disks and stores those keys in Key Vault as its standard design — unlike Storage Service Encryption or TDE, which default to Microsoft-managed keys with CMK as an optional upgrade.

questions.q: A compliance framework requires that the customer be able to independently cut off access to their own stored data at any time, without involving the cloud provider. What does this point to?
options: This is already guaranteed by platform-managed encryption, no change needed
A requirement to disable encryption at rest so the customer can manage access directly
A requirement for a customer-managed key, since revoking the key's access policy makes the encrypted data unreadable on demand
A requirement to move the data out of the cloud entirely
questions.explain: Independent, on-demand revocation of access to data is exactly the capability a customer-managed key provides — the customer controls the key's access policy in Key Vault or KMS and can revoke it without any action from the provider.
